newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan banks seek higher return on forex deposits.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan banks seek higher return on forex deposits.

text.p: The flow of foreign currency deposits into cash-strapped Pakistan may slow unless the rate of return is increased, bankers said on Monday.
The return on dollar deposits is currently 0.5 percent above the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR).

"The return should be at least two percent above LIBOR if Pakistan wants to attract more foreign currency deposits at a faster pace," Maqsood Ahmad, vice-president of the private Muslim Commercial Bank, told Reuters.
He said the number of institutional investors willing to lend foreign currency to Pakistan dropped sharply after Moody's Investors Service cut its credit ratings on November 6.

"The few lenders left are seeking higher returns," Ahmad said. Banks were unable to borrow abroad at less than 1.5 percent above LIBOR because the downgrade by Moody's had increased Pakistan's country risk.

Moody's lowered Pakistan's sovereign ceiling for foreign currency loans to B2 from B1. Its ceiling for foreign currency bank deposits was cut to B3 from B2 and Moody's said it was possible this rating would be further downgraded.

A foreign banker, who asked not to be named, said bankers had suggested at a meeting on Saturday with Shahid Javed Burki, adviser on finance and economic affairs, that returns should be raised for banks bringing in deposits of at least $10 million.
The State (central) Bank of Pakistan (SBP) on Sunday extended to December 10 the deadline for a high-yield concessionary scheme to banks bringing in forex deposits.

In October, SBP governor Muhammad Yaqub offered a 17 percent annual return on the rupee equivalent of foreign currency deposits brought by banks from abroad between October 22 and November 28 in a bid to replenish depleted reserves.
Foreign reserves, excluding gold and special drawing rights, fell to $573 million on October 31 but rose to $670 million on November 7, according to SBP figures.
The central bank also withdrew on Sunday an earlier restriction that the 17 percent return would only be applicable to any increase in banks' forex deposits as of October 22.
Bankers said the cost of borrowing from international markets added to the cost of transactions, including a 10 percent withholding tax, and this had kept inflows slow.
They said the SBP's restriction that the funds committed to the 17 percent scheme could not be swapped into rupees and invested in government paper had also dampened enthusiasm.

Ahmad said the actual return after accounting for the cost of investment was no more than 14 percent, which he said was not fair given that the SBP was charging 20 percent on repurchase (repo) discounting and offering six-month bonds at 15 percent.
The SBP auctioned six-month federal bonds worth a total of 2.88 billion rupees in a special open market operation on Sunday at a maximum cut-off of 15 percent a year.

Bankers say Pakistan's liquid foreign reserves, now at $670 million, could reach $1 billion by December, but it was not clear if the rise could be sustained unless banks bringing in foreign currency are compensated for the higher country risk. ($1 = 40 rupees)
